title: LuminousMoth
summary: LuminousMoth is an espionage intrusion set that public reporting, including work by several vendors, associates with Chinese-nexus interests and describes as active since around 2020. Its documented focus is government organisations in Southeast Asia, particularly Myanmar and the Philippines, although later reporting records activity reaching beyond that region. The group is best known for two behaviours that are easy to overlook. First, it delivers a small loader disguised as a document that appears to open normally, because a decoy file is created and opened alongside the malicious code, so the victim sees what they expect. Second, it has conducted unusually large-scale collection of browser data, saved credentials, and files from removable drives, which nets huge volumes of material across many victims at once rather than a narrow select few. Tooling overlaps with commercial penetration testing frameworks and commodity loaders have been reported in the chain. The combination of volume and the decoy document trick means user reports are rare, and defenders usually discover the activity through egress volume or endpoint telemetry.

beginner.definition: LuminousMoth is the name for a group of attackers that public reports link to Chinese state interests. Those reports say it has targeted government offices in Southeast Asia since about 2020. Later activity reached other regions as well. It is known for stealing large amounts of data from many machines at once. It also hides behind files that look completely normal.
beginner.whyItMatters: When you open the file, a real document appears on your screen. Nothing looks broken, so you carry on with your day. Underneath, a small program has already started. Because you saw nothing strange, you may never report it, and your security team never gets a warning. The group then gathers browser passwords and files from memory sticks in bulk. That can turn a handful of infected laptops into thousands of stolen logins, and those logins often unlock other systems.
howItWorks: The attackers send a message with a link or a file that looks like an ordinary document.
When it opens, a genuine decoy document appears so the reader notices nothing wrong.
At the same time, a hidden loader starts and fetches more tools from the internet.
The extra tools copy saved browser passwords, cookies, and other stored data.
They also scan removable drives and copy documents from any they find.
Everything is bundled and uploaded in large transfers that stand out in network logs.
beginner.example: Think of a magician who shakes your hand with his right hand while his left hand takes your wallet. You felt a handshake, and you saw nothing else, so you never check your pocket. The decoy document is the handshake. The hidden loader is the other hand, and your browser passwords are the wallet. Because the trick feels friendly and normal, you are unlikely to raise an alarm.
takeaways: A document that opens normally tells you nothing about whether it was safe.
Protect credentials stored in browsers, because they are a favourite and easily stolen target.
Report unexpected files even when they appear to work fine, since that is exactly the disguise.

objectives: Explain how a decoy document reduces the chance that a victim reports an infection.
Describe why bulk credential and removable drive collection is more damaging than a single theft.
Identify network evidence that indicates unusually large outbound data transfers.
Explain the practical limits of trusting a document simply because it opens correctly.
Summarise how public reporting describes this group's attribution and regional scope.
Recommend user actions that make browser stored credentials less attractive to steal.
